title: ‘indi — having, and numbers up to twenty
goal: Say what you have and don't have, count to twenty, and understand why Arabic has no verb "to have" at all.
bekal: use عِنْد and negate it with مَا
count from one to twenty and count things
tell apart عِنْد · فِي and مَع, three words with close meanings

dialogs.title: حَكِي — بِالسَّكَن
dialogs.intro: Budi has just moved into a rented room and is checking it out with the landlord, Abu Sami.

lines.speaker: أَبُو سَامِي:
lines.id: Here you are, this is the room.

lines.speaker: أَبُو سَامِي:
lines.baca: akiid fi. w fi barraad kamaan.
lines.id: Of course there is. And there's a fridge too.
lines.literal: sure there-is. and there-is fridge too.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Good. How many rooms are there in the house?

lines.speaker: أَبُو سَامِي:
lines.text: أَرْبَع أُوَض. تْلَاتِة مَأْجُورِين وْوَحْدِة فَاضْيِة.
lines.baca: arba‘ ōwaḍ. tlaate ma’juuriin w wahde faaḍye.
lines.id: Four rooms. Three are rented and one is empty.
lines.literal: four rooms. three rented and one empty.

lines.speaker: أَبُو سَامِي:
lines.text: إِيه، بَسّ مَا عِنَّا وَاي فَاي بِكِلّ أُوضَة.
lines.baca: ēh, bass ma ‘inna waay faay bikill ōḍa.
lines.id: Yes, but we don't have wifi in every room.
lines.literal: yes, but not at-us wifi in-every room.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: That's OK. I have a SIM card from the phone company.

lines.speaker: أَبُو سَامِي:
lines.id: Good. Do you have money on you now?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: مَعِي مِيتَين، بَسّ مَا مَعِي أَكْتَر.
lines.baca: ma‘i miitēn, bass ma ma‘i aktar.
lines.id: I have two hundred on me, but no more.
lines.literal: with-me two-hundred, but not with-me more.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Thanks. I have one more question.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: فِي مَحَلّ قَرِيب؟ بَدِّي خُبْز وْمَي.
lines.baca: fi mahall ’ariib? baddi khubz w mayy.
lines.id: Is there a shop nearby? I want bread and water.
lines.literal: there-is shop near? want-my bread and water.

lines.speaker: أَبُو سَامِي:
lines.text: إِيه، تْحِت عَ الزَّاوِيِة. مَفْتُوح لَلْعَشَرَة.
lines.id: Yes, downstairs on the corner. It's open until ten.

notes: **Arabic has no verb "to have" at all.** Instead it uses the preposition عِنْد ("at") plus a possessive ending: عِنْدِي *‘indi* means "at me", and that's how you say "I have". This isn't a gap in the language — Russian and Turkish do the same thing.
**Because عِنْد isn't a noun, its negative is مَا, not مِش.** The correct form is مَا عِنْدِي *ma ‘indi*. The form مِش عِنْدِي sounds wrong straight away, although it's still understood.

**Three similar words, and the difference matters.** The word عِنْدِي means "I have" in general; مَعِي *ma‘i* means "I have it on me"; فِي *fi* means "there is", without naming an owner. The answer عِنْدِي مَصَارِي may mean your money is in the bank, while مَعِي مَصَارِي means it's in your pocket right now.

**Numbers three to ten use a short form in front of a noun.** The stand-alone form تْلَاتِة becomes تْلَات when a noun follows: تْلَات أُوَض *tlaat ōwaḍ* ("three rooms"). The long form is used for counting on its own or giving a number.
**From eleven up, the noun goes back to singular.** The phrase خَمْسْتَعْش كْتَاب is literally "fifteen book (singular)". That actually makes life easier — no plural to worry about.

**The replies مَاشِي and مَاشِي الْحَال mean "that's fine", not "walking".** It's one of the most frequent expressions in the Levant, used to accept a situation, agree to a suggestion, or calm someone's worries.

grammars.title: The words عِنْد, مَع and فِي
after: Notice the irregular "we" form: عِنَّا *‘inna*, not عِنْدْنَا. Its د has melted away. It's the only form that breaks the pattern — and the one you'll use most when talking about your family.
To ask a question, nothing changes — just raise your voice: عِنْدَك وَقْت؟ ("do you have time?"). The short answers are إِيه، عِنْدِي or لَا، مَا عِنْدِي.

grammars.title: Numbers from one to twenty
after: ⚠️ For **two**, Arabic doesn't use the number but changes the noun: كْتَاب becomes كْتَابَين *ktaabēn* ("two books"), يَوْم becomes يَوْمَين *yōmēn* ("two days"). This form is called the *muthanna* (dual), and in dialect it's much simpler than in Fusha: just add ـَين.
For **one**, the number goes **after** the noun and is often left out altogether: كْتَاب means "a book" with nothing added. The word وَاحِد is used only when you want to stress "just one".

head: Sentence
Say it
Meaning
rows: I don't have a single book

blocks.text: The last row shows how to make a negative emphatic: the word وَلَا before the noun means "not a single one". It's much stronger than مَا عِنْدِي كْتُب, and works just like "not a single…" in English.

blocks.title: Three plural forms to accept as they are
items: Arabic plurals can hardly be guessed from the singular: كْتَاب becomes كْتُب · بَيْت becomes بْيُوت · وَلَد becomes وْلَاد · أُوضَة becomes أُوَض.
The good news at A1: you **don't need to produce them**. You only need to recognize them when you hear them, and learn the plurals of the ten to fifteen most common words.
Feminine nouns often form the plural just by adding ـَات, and that's the easiest kind: سَاعَة becomes سَاعَات · مَجَلِّة becomes مَجَلَّات · سَيَّارَة becomes سَيَّارَات.

blocks.text: The word مَي *mayy* is one of the most frequent words in the whole Levant, and it's far from the Fusha مَاء. If you say the Fusha form, people will understand, but you'll instantly sound like you're reading aloud.

blocks.title: Asking whether something is available
items: There's just one formula: فِي + thing + ؟ — for example فِي مَي سُخْنِة؟ ("is there hot water?").
A yes is simply إِيه، فِي. A no is لَا، مَا فِي. No need to repeat the thing.
If you're asking about a place rather than a thing, swap فِي for وَين — for example وَين الْمَحَلّ؟ ("where's the shop?").
I don't have money on me.
